fixes.explanation: That's the third group, baker. The psalm says, “Let those who fear the LORD say…” (Psalm 118:4). First comes Israel, then the house of Aaron, then those who fear the LORD. Same line each time, and a new group saying it.

The text says otherwise, friend. “All the nations surrounded me, but in the name of the LORD I cut them off.” (Psalm 118:10). He cut them off, and he did it in the name of the LORD. So the verse says it plainly, and True is the answer.

Ooh, close but no, friend. The verse says, “The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation.” (Psalm 118:14). Salvation is right there in the line, and the LORD is the One who has become it. Say it with me: He has become my salvation.

Not quite, friend. Right after the cornerstone line, the writer says, “This is from the LORD, and it is marvelous in our eyes.” (Psalm 118:23). He gives the LORD the credit, and he calls it marvelous. Go ahead and marvel right along with him.
The psalm says nothing about kings getting rich or strong. The reason is the LORD's loving devotion, which is great toward us (Psalm 117:2). That's the one the writer gives.

Hold on, friend, I think the word distress threw you. The writer says, “In my distress I called to the LORD, and He answered and set me free.” (Psalm 118:5). He called, the LORD answered, and he was set free. Not one word about him staying stuck.
Worry is nowhere in this verse. He says, “The LORD is on my side; I will not be afraid.” So the question that follows isn't a worried one. I think he's asking it with confidence.

You got it, baker. “It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in man.” (Psalm 118:8). The next verse says it again about princes: “It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in princes.” (Psalm 118:9). Same refuge both times, and it's the LORD.

Sheep aren't in this verse, friend. The text says the nations “…were extinguished like burning thorns…” (Psalm 118:12). The bees are how the writer pictures them swarming, and the thorns are how he pictures what happened to them.

A river isn't in this picture, friend. The psalm says, “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” (Psalm 118:22). It never mentions a river. What it says is that the rejected stone has become the cornerstone.

Quiet isn't what the verse names, friend. The text says, “we will rejoice and be glad in it.” (Psalm 118:24). Rejoicing and being glad are what the writer says we will do in the day the LORD has made.

That's right, baker. The psalm says, “The LORD is God; He has made His light to shine upon us.” (Psalm 118:27). I spent years in the dark of a junk drawer, so I'll tell you light is a big deal. And this is the light He made to shine upon us.
